record.title: Paper finds asynchronous delivery order can change search agents’ acquired evidence and proposes schedule-stable coordination
record.summary: A preprint reports that changing the delivery order of identical evidence packets can alter what search agents retrieve, with the difference persisting after all initial evidence arrives and through another search. Across controlled QA tasks, early commitment produced 11.6–23.8 percentage points of acquisition disagreement above same-order repeat variation in eight model-task settings. The paper proposes Confluent Evidence Acquisition (CEA), which waits for each subquestion’s assigned evidence and uses a schedule-independent rule to allocate shared searches. In question-only plans, the authors report acquisition disagreement near repeat variation across three benchmarks; accuracy was comparable to a complete-input control and improved over early commitment on 2Wiki and HotpotQA, but not MuSiQue. These are author-reported results in a frozen-corpus QA setting, not an independently reproduced finding or a demonstration across deployed agents.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The inspected preprint reports controlled experiments in which changing the delivery order of identical evidence packets redirected search choices; the reported acquisition disagreement persisted after input completion and through a second search.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Across eight model-task settings, early commitment produced 11.6–23.8 percentage points of excess acquisition disagreement over same-order repeat variation. With question-only plans, the authors report that CEA reduced disagreement to 0.6, -0.2 and 1.0 points on 2Wiki, HotpotQA and MuSiQue, respectively.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In the question-only-plan evaluation, the preprint reports that CEA improved accuracy over early commitment by 12.6 percentage points on 2Wiki and 3.6 points on HotpotQA, with a -0.1-point change on MuSiQue; results were comparable to the complete-input shared-history control.

claims.label: INFERRED
claims.text: When tool results arrive asynchronously, completion-order scheduling can affect which evidence supports later reasoning, so evidence provenance and scheduler policy may need to be audited together.

evidence_gaps.description: The schedule-permutation and CEA results have not been independently reproduced, and no code artifact was inspected in this review.
The effect of asynchronous scheduling on evidence acquisition in open-web research and production agent runtimes is unknown.
The practical frequency and size of contention-induced acquisition divergence under real shared retrieval budgets are not reported.

brief.importance_rationale: If robust beyond the reported controlled QA regime, schedule-dependent evidence acquisition could affect reproducibility, support recovery and auditability across tool-using agents, while a dependency-aware schedule-independent allocator offers a practical control. It is broadly relevant enough to track but remains a single preprint on three frozen-corpus QA benchmarks, not demonstrated in open-ended research or deployment.
limitations: This is one author-reported preprint; the research desk did not independently reproduce the experiments or verify the formal claims.
The evaluations use frozen corpora and multi-hop QA tasks, not open-web research, changing source quality, long-running autonomous projects or deployed organizational workflows.

Most controlled results use DeepSeek-V4-Flash; cross-model checks use fixed subsets and GPT-5.6 Luna. Generalization to other model families, schedulers, tool APIs and runtime architectures is unknown.

The papers' estimated excess-disagreement measures depend on two repeats per order, selected questions and the authors' target-category/document-set metrics; other evidence-quality and provenance measures could yield different conclusions.
Question-only plans and retrieval-call ownership structure CEA's dependency domains. More complex plans, shared evidence dependencies and dynamically changing evidence were not established here.
The 21.6-point first-ready allocation effect is a high-contention setup with two missing supports and one shared search slot; ordinary contention frequency and production impact are unknown.

The timed comparison reports small final-response reductions in the measured staggered-delivery tasks; simultaneous arrival gives essentially no speedup, and external tool-service costs are not fully charged.
brief.summary: A preprint reports that changing the delivery order of identical evidence packets can alter what search agents retrieve, with the difference persisting after all initial evidence arrives and through another search. Across controlled QA tasks, early commitment produced 11.6–23.8 percentage points of acquisition disagreement above same-order repeat variation in eight model-task settings. The paper proposes Confluent Evidence Acquisition (CEA), which waits for each subquestion’s assigned evidence and uses a schedule-independent rule to allocate shared searches. In question-only plans, the authors report acquisition disagreement near repeat variation across three benchmarks; accuracy was comparable to a complete-input control and improved over early commitment on 2Wiki and HotpotQA, but not MuSiQue. These are author-reported results in a frozen-corpus QA setting, not an independently reproduced finding or a demonstration across deployed agents.

technical.claimed_result: On frozen-corpus multi-hop QA, the authors report that early-delivery schedules changed search acquisitions and that CEA reduced acquisition disagreement to near repeat variation while matching complete-input accuracy, with task-specific gains over early commitment. Under high shared-budget contention, first-ready allocation added 21.6 percentage points of acquisition disagreement.
technical.compute_or_cost: The paper reports model calls, input tokens and latency in selected matched comparisons; it does not establish full external retrieval/tool-service costs or a production-level economic comparison.
technical.demonstrated_result: The paper and its appendices establish that the authors report paired schedule-permutation experiments, same-order repeat controls, acquisition-disagreement measures, answer-accuracy comparisons and a formal invariance result under a fixed plan and stable conditional response law. the research desk did not reproduce the experimental outcomes or proof.
technical.implementation_status: Preprint proposes and evaluates CEA in controlled experiments; no production implementation or deployment result was inspected.
technical.mechanism: Confluent Evidence Acquisition (CEA) assigns initial retrieved documents to dependency domains for subquestions. Each branch reasons when its assigned evidence is complete, without waiting for unrelated branches; a schedule-independent allocation rule chooses among search requests competing for a shared search budget. This separates evidence dependencies from execution timing.
technical.novelty: The paper treats evidence-acquisition reproducibility as distinct from answer accuracy and identifies both evidence-arrival timing and shared-budget allocation as schedule-dependent routes to different acquired support. CEA combines dependency-scoped reasoning with schedule-independent search allocation.
technical.regime: Frozen BM25 corpora and multi-hop QA from 2Wiki, HotpotQA and MuSiQue; primary experiments use DeepSeek-V4-Flash (temperature 0, non-thinking), with cross-model comparisons on fixed subsets using GPT-5.6 Luna at low reasoning effort. Delivery orders are permuted; each order is repeated twice. The main CEA question-only-plan table uses 100 questions per benchmark.
technical.reproducibility: Protocol, datasets, settings and appendices are described in the preprint, but the research desk did not run the experiments or independently verify the formal result. No code repository was inspected during this review.
technical.strongest_baseline: Matched complete-input shared-history controls and early commitment after two arrivals, with identical questions, evidence packets, retriever and model settings; same-order repeated runs estimate stochastic variation. The paper also compares fixed-priority CEA allocation with first-ready allocation under low and high search contention.

brief.title: Paper finds asynchronous delivery order can change search agents’ acquired evidence and proposes schedule-stable coordination
brief.why_it_matters: The paper separates answer accuracy from reproducibility of the evidence path: two runs can receive the same information overall yet acquire different support because asynchronous timing changes which search happens first. If this mechanism generalizes, scheduler and tool-allocation choices become part of research-agent evidence selection and auditability. CEA suggests a design that lets independent reasoning progress while stabilizing both subquestion evidence and shared search allocation. Current evidence is limited to controlled multi-hop QA tasks and one preprint, so transfer to open-web research, production agents, other schedulers and real operating costs remains unestablished.
